title: Apply the principles of customer care in client interactions

lessons.title: Who your customers are and what they expect
lessons.html:
Internal and external customers

In the perishable produce industry, a customer is anyone who depends on your work. There are two kinds:

  • External customers: overseas importers, retailers, local buyers, growers who use your packhouse or cold store, and transport companies.
  • Internal customers: people inside the business who rely on you, such as the dispatch team who needs packed pallets on time, or the QC department who needs accurate records.

Treating internal customers well makes it possible to serve external customers well. If the packing line supervisor does not tell the cold store when pallets are coming, the cold store cannot have space ready and the exporter's container may be late.

What customers expect

  • Reliability: doing what was promised, on time, every time.
  • Quality: product that meets the agreed specification.
  • Responsiveness: quick answers to questions and problems.
  • Respect and courtesy: being treated politely and taken seriously.
  • Accurate information: correct documents, quantities and updates.
  • Fairness: honest dealing when things go wrong.

Why customer care matters

Fresh produce is a relationship business. Buyers have many suppliers to choose from. A packhouse with a reputation for honest, clear communication keeps its growers and buyers for years. A single badly handled complaint can lose a client worth millions of rand.

Good customer care also makes work easier: fewer disputes, fewer urgent phone calls and a better working environment.

First impressions

How you answer the phone, greet a visiting buyer or respond to an email creates an impression of the whole business. Greet people by name, introduce yourself, listen without interrupting, and make sure the person knows what will happen next.

lessons.title: Communicating and handling complaints
lessons.html:
Effective communication with clients

  • Listen actively: give full attention, take notes and repeat back the main points to confirm you understood.
  • Ask questions: open questions (what, how, when) help you understand the need.
  • Be clear: use simple language; avoid jargon with clients who are not from the industry.
  • Confirm in writing: follow up phone calls with an email or message summarising what was agreed.
  • Respect differences: clients may come from different cultures and speak different first languages. Be patient and polite.
  • Keep promises: if you say you will call back by three o'clock, do it, even if only to say you need more time.

Handling a complaint step by step

  1. Listen calmly without interrupting or arguing.
  2. Acknowledge the problem and the client's feelings: I understand this delay causes you a problem.
  3. Apologise for the inconvenience, without blaming others.
  4. Get the facts: pallet numbers, dates, photos, temperature records.
  5. Agree on a solution within your authority, or escalate to the right person.
  6. Follow up to make sure the problem was solved.
  7. Record the complaint and its cause so it does not happen again.

Example

A grower phones angrily because his bins waited four hours at the packhouse gate in the sun. The receiving clerk listens, apologises, checks the receiving log and finds that the forklift was broken. She explains this, tells him the forklift has been repaired, and arranges with the supervisor that his next delivery gets priority. She records the complaint so management can plan a back-up forklift.

Difficult situations

Stay calm and professional even if the client is rude. Never make promises you cannot keep. If a client becomes abusive, politely end the conversation and involve your manager.

Key points

  • Customers can be external or internal.
  • Customers expect reliability, quality, responsiveness, respect and accurate information.
  • Listen actively and confirm agreements in writing.
  • Handle complaints: listen, acknowledge, apologise, get facts, solve, follow up and record.
  • Stay professional and escalate when needed.

quiz.question: Which of these is an internal customer?

options.text: The dispatch team that needs packed pallets on time

quiz.question: What is the first step in handling a complaint?

options.text: Explain why the client is wrong

quiz.question: Why should you confirm phone agreements in writing?

options.text: To avoid misunderstandings about what was agreed

quiz.question: You promised to call back by three o'clock but do not have an answer yet. What should you do?

options.text: Wait until you have the answer, however long it takes
Ask a colleague to say you are out
Call by three to say you need more time

quiz.question: What should be done after a complaint has been resolved?

options.text: Record it and its cause so it does not happen again
